scenario.name: Rhysida Ransomware SilentKill PowerShell Preparation, PortStarter & LibTomCrypt AES-CTR (AA23-319A)
scenario.overview: Imagine a bustling coastal shipping port with blue harbor water, stacked colorful steel cargo containers, a towering yellow overhead gantry crane, and a moored cargo ship. Out on the concrete harbor pier, a worker notices a single shipping container whose side inspection hatch was accidentally left unlatched during loading. In this real-world scenario, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the stacked cargo containers & ship, then smuggles copied records out past the harbor crane inspection pier in tiny disguised batches. The port authority watchtower spots footsteps leaving a supposedly sealed container bay and compares the manifest seal numbers against the pier camera. In this scenario (T1562.004, Rhysida Ransomware SilentKill PowerShell Preparation, PortStarter & LibTomCrypt AES-CTR (AA23-319A)) on DEV-0832, the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: portStarter Golang Backdoor, then silentKill PowerShell Script Disabling 200+, then multi-Threaded LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering PortStarter Golang Backdoor, then SilentKill PowerShell Script Disabling 200+, then Multi-Threaded LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.subtitle: Persistence & Defense Evasion (T1562.004 - Disable or Modify System Firewall)
stages.description: Out on the concrete harbor pier, a worker notices a single shipping container whose side inspection hatch was accidentally left unlatched during loading. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the stacked cargo containers & ship while everyday visitors and the harbor customs inspector go about their routine. After initial VPN or credential access, the operator installed PortStarter (a custom Golang backdoor shared between Vice Society and Rhysida affiliates that registers itself as a Windows service and executes netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Windows Update Service" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=49155 to punch an inbound hole in the host firewall for encrypted C2 communication). The shared use of PortStarter and SilentKill provided high-confidence forensic proof that Vice Society (DEV-0832) operators transitioned directly to the Rhysida ransomware payload in mid-2023. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Rhysida Affiliate (Vice Society Nexus) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Windows Update Service" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=49155 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: SilentKill PowerShell Script (g.ps1) Disabling 200+ Services & Unhooking AMSI). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="Windows Update Service" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=49155 / ⇠#1 ACK 1) from Node ① (#1 Rhysida Affiliate (Vice Society Nexus)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR (.rhysida)).

stages.title: Stage 2: SilentKill PowerShell Script (g.ps1) Disabling 200+ Services & Unhooking AMSI
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion & Service Stop (T1562.001 / T1489)
stages.description: Slipping out through that open container hatch while the yellow gantry crane swings overhead, the stowaway steps straight onto the restricted customs dockyard. Here in Step 2 inside the shipping port, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the stacked cargo containers & ship without disturbing the sealed bonded export yard. To prepare the environment for unobstructed encryption, the operator ran SilentKill (g.ps1), which first patched AmsiScanBuffer in amsi.dll memory, iterated through a hardcoded list of over 200 Windows services (Stop-Service -Force targeting Sophos, Symantec, Veeam, SQL Server, Exchange, and shadow copies so database files were unlocked for encryption), and set HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\DisableRestrictedAdmin = 0 (enabling RestrictedAdmin RDP mode so the attacker could log into downstream servers via RDP using NTLM password hashes without cleartext passwords). Enabling DisableRestrictedAdmin = 0 across the domain allows the operator to Pass-the-Hash over RDP (mstsc.exe /restrictedadmin) without exposing their own cleartext credentials on target hosts. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ powershell.exe / ⇠#2 ALERT 4104) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 PortStarter Go Backdoor (Firewall Rule)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR (.rhysida)).

stages.title: Stage 3: Multi-Threaded LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR Encryption & Desktop Wallpaper Lock (.rhysida)
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact / T1491.001 - Internal Defacement)
stages.description: Now roaming freely outside the sealed steel box, the intruder walks across the shipping port pier and alters manifests bound for the moored cargo ship. In this final step inside the shipping port, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the harbor crane inspection pier in tiny disguised batches until the port authority manifest watch catches the mismatch. Pushed domain-wide via psexec.exe -d -s, the 64-bit MinGW-compiled rhysida.exe binary invoked its statically linked LibTomCrypt v1.18.2 cryptographic library (aes_setup and ctr_start in AES-256-CTR mode paired with a hardcoded 4096-bit RSA public key) to encrypt files across all local drives, appending .rhysida, writing a PDF ransom note (CriticalBreachDetected.pdf), and modifying HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper to display an extortion warning. Unlike most ransomware families that drop .txt or .hta ransom notes, Rhysida generates a standalone .pdf document (CriticalBreachDetected.pdf) in every encrypted directory. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ rhysida.exe / ⇠#3 ACK 11) from Node ③ (#3 PortStarter Go Backdoor (Firewall Rule)) to Node ④ (#4 SilentKill PowerShell Script (g.ps1)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 LibTomCrypt AES-256-CTR (.rhysida)).
